holidays.name: National Frozen Yogurt Day
holidays.description: A day to celebrate the tangy, creamy, swirl-it-yourself dessert that lets you feel virtuous while piling on a mountain of gummy bears and cookie dough. Self-serve toppings bars are the true stars of the celebration.
holidays.origin: An unofficial food holiday observed in the United States, popularized by food-day calendars and frozen yogurt shops that use it to promote deals and free samples.
holidays.funFact: Frozen yogurt surged in popularity in the 1980s when it was marketed as a healthier alternative to ice cream, and the self-serve frozen yogurt boom of the 2010s made 'pay by weight' a household concept.

holidays.name: Take Your Child to the Library Day
holidays.description: Held on the first Saturday of February, this observance encourages families to visit the library together, get library cards, and discover that books, movies, and free Wi-Fi are all waiting there for the borrowing.
holidays.origin: Started in 2002 by author Mary Jo Fedorko? No: it was launched by librarians and literacy advocates in the United States to promote early reading habits and make libraries part of family routines.
holidays.funFact: Many libraries now lend far more than books, including tools, board games, telescopes, seeds, and even fishing poles.

holidays.name: Bubble Gum Day
holidays.description: A sticky-sweet day for blowing bubbles, popping them loudly, and contemplating the eternal question of whether you should really stick gum under a table. Contests for the biggest bubble are encouraged, face-splatters are not.
holidays.origin: An unofficial food and candy observance that appears on novelty holiday calendars, celebrating the chewy treat that has been a pop culture staple for generations.
holidays.funFact: The Guinness World Record for the largest bubble gum bubble blown is over 20 inches in diameter, and it was blown without using hands.

holidays.name: Waitangi Day
holidays.description: New Zealand's national day, marked with ceremonies, cultural performances, community events, and plenty of barbecues, held on the anniversary of a founding document in the country's history.
holidays.origin: It commemorates the signing of the Treaty of Waitangi on February 6, 1840, between representatives of the British Crown and many Māori chiefs. It became a public holiday in the 1970s.
holidays.funFact: The Treaty exists in both English and Māori versions, and differences between the two texts have been debated and examined by courts and tribunals for generations.

holidays.name: Ldevelopment Day: Lame Duck Day
holidays.description: A day to salute the lame duck: that outgoing politician or lagging project with limited time left. It is a gentle reminder to give a little grace to anyone limping toward the finish line.
holidays.origin: Observed on February 6 in some novelty calendars, tied to the 20th Amendment ratification on February 6, 1933, which shortened the period between US elections and the start of new terms.
holidays.funFact: The 20th Amendment moved Inauguration Day from March 4 to January 20, cutting the 'lame duck' period of presidents by about six weeks.
